candidate.title: The Origins of Alchemy in Graeco-Roman Egypt (chyma, 'to pour', section on the name alchemy)
candidate.venue: Frederick Muller, London (scan on Internet Archive)
candidate.ask_addressed: What is the evidence and scholarly status of the claim that the word 'chemistry'/'alchemy' derives from Kemet/Khem/'black land' (Egyptian kmt)? What are the competing etymologies (Greek chyma/cheo, Arabic kimiya, others) and who argues which? State clearly which is most widely accepted and why.
candidate.quote: this fact gives it a great claim to underlie the name of Alchemy.
candidate.summary: Argues chymia/chymeia comes from Greek cheein 'pour' and chyma 'ingot, bar' (attested 3rd-century BC Oropos inscription, 2nd-century Delos), so the name arises from metallurgy. Notes that the earlier form of the word cannot be proved because no early texts exist.
candidate.limits: Secondary, 1970; the inscriptional evidence is reported, not examined here. Not a consensus statement; Lindsay himself says there is no proof which form was earlier. Stance lowered from supports: the page supports the Greek chyma derivation, not the Kmt claim the ask addresses, and Lindsay hedges that it is not proof.
